comparisons.peer_summary: USPB net income was $1.4 billion, a 24% decrease from the prior year, primarily driven by higher cost of credit which was partially offset by higher revenues and lower expenses.
comparisons.comparison: Both Bank of America (BAC) and Citigroup (C) report a decline in segment net income for 2024 driven by a combination of negative drivers (provision for credit losses/cost of credit) and revenue/expense pressures. BAC's Deposits segment net income decreased $1.2 billion to $7.5 billion, attributed to lower revenue and higher noninterest expense, partially offset by lower provision for credit losses. Conversely, C's USPB segment net income decreased 24% to $1.4 billion, primarily driven by higher cost of credit, which was partially offset by higher revenues and lower expenses. While both experienced net income declines, the primary drag for BAC was operational (revenue/expense mix) aided by credit improvements, whereas C's primary drag was credit-related, aided by operational efficiency.

USPB net income of $1.4 billion decreased 24%, driven by higher cost of credit, partially offset by higher revenues and lower expenses.

comparisons.peer_summary: Provision for credit losses increased to $1.54 billion in 2024 from $1.14 billion in 2023, primarily driven by net charge-offs in the credit card portfolio.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures address the provision for credit losses as a significant financial measure within their MD&A. BAC explicitly cites 'lower provision for credit losses' as a positive offsetting factor that helped mitigate the decline in its Deposits segment net income. GS provides a detailed breakdown of its overall provision for credit losses, noting an increase to $1.54 billion from $1.14 billion, primarily driven by net charge-offs in the credit card portfolio. The comparison highlights divergent credit trends: BAC benefited from a reduction in credit provisions at the segment level, while GS reported a substantial increase in credit provisions at the platform level.

sentences.text: Net income for Deposits decreased $1.2 billion to $7.5 billion primarily due to lower revenue and higher noninterest expense, partially offset by lower provision for credit losses.
Provision for credit losses was $1.54 billion for 2024, compared with $1.14 billion for 2023.
Provisions for 2024 reflected net provisions related to the credit card portfolio (primarily driven by net charge-offs).

comparisons.peer_summary: Noninterest expense was $35.4 billion, up 4%, driven by higher compensation expense (including revenue-related compensation and increased headcount) and higher technology and brokerage expense, partially offset by lower legal expense.
comparisons.comparison: Both BAC and JPMorgan Chase (JPM) identify higher noninterest expense as a key driver of financial performance changes in 2024. BAC attributes its Deposits segment net income decrease partly to 'higher noninterest expense.' JPM reports that its overall noninterest expense increased 4% to $35.4 billion, driven by higher compensation expense (including revenue-related compensation and increased headcount) and higher technology/brokerage expense. This indicates a shared industry pressure on operating costs, specifically labor and technology, impacting net income.
